nameStory: The name "Tickseed Sunflower" comes from the plant's flat, seed-like fruits that were thought to resemble tiny ticks clinging to clothing and fur. The "sunflower" part refers to its bright yellow daisy-like blooms that belong to the same plant family as true sunflowers. Some folks also call plants in this genus "beggarticks" because the seeds stick to you like a persistent beggar!
description: Tickseed Sunflower is a tall annual wildflower that can reach up to 40 inches in height, creating impressive golden displays in wet areas during late summer. It produces cheerful yellow flowers that look like small sunflowers, with bright yellow petals (called ray petals) surrounding a darker yellow center. This wetland lover thrives in marshy spots and flood plains, often forming colonies that light up the landscape. Like other members of the beggarticks family, it's both beautiful to look at and notorious for its hitchhiking seeds.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow daisy-like flowers with 6-10 yellow petals surrounding a yellow center disc, typically producing up to 3 flower heads per branch that feel papery when touched

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall annual herb reaching 2-3 feet high with branching stems that feel somewhat rough and angular to the touch

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Leaves are arranged in opposite pairs along the stem and often have a slightly rough, sandpapery texture when rubbed between fingers

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Flat, wedge-shaped seeds with 2-4 barbed bristles that grab onto clothing and fur with remarkable tenacity - you'll feel them sticking before you see them

idTips.label: Habitat Preference
idTips.description: Almost always found in wet or periodically flooded areas like marsh edges, pond shores, and ditches where the soil stays moist

habitat: In New England, look for Tickseed Sunflower along the edges of marshes, ponds, and slow-moving streams, especially in areas that flood seasonally. It thrives in disturbed wet soils like roadside ditches, abandoned farm fields that stay soggy, and the muddy shores of reservoirs. You'll often find it growing alongside other wetland plants like cattails, sedges, and other beggarticks species.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate in late spring when soil warms, producing small seedlings with their first opposite leaves in wet, muddy areas.
seasonality.summer: Plants grow rapidly through summer, developing tall branching stems but typically not flowering until late in the season.
seasonality.fall: Bright yellow flowers bloom from late August through October, followed quickly by the production of those famously sticky seeds that will cling to your clothes.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems may persist through winter in protected areas, but the annual plants die completely, leaving only seeds to sprout the following spring.

funFact: The sticky seeds of Tickseed Sunflower are so effective at hitchhiking that they've been known to travel hundreds of miles on migrating waterfowl, essentially turning ducks and geese into unwitting long-distance gardeners who plant new colonies wherever they stop to rest!
confusionNotes: Tickseed Sunflower is extremely similar to Bearded Beggarticks and they actually interbreed where their ranges overlap, making identification quite tricky even for experts. The key difference is subtle - Tickseed Sunflower typically has fewer, broader outer bracts around the flower head. Memory trick: if you're not sure which beggarticks you're looking at in a wet area, you're probably looking at one of these two closely related species!
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this plant with the popular garden flowers also called "tickseed" or "coreopsis" - those are in a different genus entirely, though they're in the same sunflower family. The beggarticks genus (Bidens) gets its scientific name from the Latin words meaning "two teeth," referring to the typically two-pronged seed bristles.
compareHints: Among New England's many beggarticks species, Tickseed Sunflower stands out for having showy yellow petals - many of its relatives like Devil's Beggarticks have tiny or no petals at all. It's most easily confused with Bearded Beggarticks, but generally grows taller and has fewer flower heads per branch. Unlike Nodding Beggarticks, its flower heads face upward rather than drooping downward.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's many beggarticks species, Devil's Beggarticks is distinguished by its three-part leaves (versus simple leaves in Nodding Beggarticks) and its lack of showy petals (unlike the bright yellow rays of Tickseed Sunflower).

Among New England's many beggarticks species, Nodding Beggarticks is the easiest to identify because of its drooping flowers - Devil's Beggarticks has upward-facing flowers and deeply divided leaves, while Smooth Beggarticks has much larger, showier flowers that face outward.
Among New England's many beggarticks species, Purplestem stands out for its smooth stems with purple coloring and relatively few flower heads per plant.
Unlike its weedy beggarticks relatives that grow in damp soil and are known for their sticky seeds, Water Marigold is the aquatic specialist of the family.
Among New England's beggarticks, Tall Beggarticks stands out for its height and hairy stems.

Unlike its freshwater cousins like Devil's Beggarticks or Nodding Beggarticks, Estuary Beggarticks has evolved to handle salt stress, giving it thicker, more succulent leaves and limiting it to coastal habitats.

Among its many Bidens relatives in New England, Smooth Beggarticks stands out for its simple, undivided leaves (unlike Three-parted Beggarticks) and its prominent yellow ray petals (unlike Devil's Beggarticks which often lacks showy petals entirely).

Among its many beggarticks relatives, swamp beggarticks stands out for its complete lack of ray petals (the showy outer petals), unlike nodding beggarticks or smooth beggarticks which have yellow rays.

Among New England beggarticks, Three-parted is unique for its deeply three-divided leaves - Devil's Beggarticks has simple oval leaves, while Spanish Needles has finely divided, almost fern-like foliage.

Among its beggarticks relatives, Spanish needles stands out with its finely divided, feathery leaves - most other Bidens species have simple oval leaves or leaves divided into just 3-5 broad segments.
Among New England's beggarticks, Bearded Beggarticks stands out for its large, showy yellow petals - most other species like Devil's Beggarticks have tiny or no petals at all.

Marsh Tickseed stands out from its beggarticks relatives by being strictly a wetland specialist - while cousins like Devil's Beggarticks grow in disturbed soils and gardens, Marsh Tickseed demands consistently soggy conditions.
Among its many beggarticks relatives, Eaton's is unique for its salt marsh habitat - most others prefer freshwater wetlands or disturbed soils.
White beggarticks stands out from its many beggarticks relatives because of its prominent white petals - most other species in the genus have small, inconspicuous flowers or yellow petals.
